content: Elective medical or surgical procedures are frequently performed on neonates admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). For these procedures, agents such as opioids are commonly used to achieve sedation, analgesia, or anaesthesia. However, the use of opioids is associated with significant adverse effects. Propofol, a sedative-hypnotic agent, is widely used in paediatric and adult populations for similar purposes. Despite its widespread use, the efficacy and safety of propofol in neonates remain undefined. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of propofol in neonates undergoing sedation or anaesthesia for procedures. Comparisons were made between propofol and placebo, no treatment, or alternative active agents. Subgroup analyses were planned based on the method of propofol administration (bolus or continuous infusion), the type of active control agent (e.g., neuromuscular blocking agents with or without sedatives, analgesics, or anxiolytics), the type of procedure (e.g., endotracheal intubation, eye examination, or other procedures), and the gestational age of the neonates (preterm versus term). To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted in MEDLINE (1950 to September 30, 2010), EMBASE (1980 to September 30, 2010), and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, The Cochrane Library 2010, Issue 2). No language restrictions were applied. Additional sources included reference lists of identified articles, abstracts submitted to Pediatric Academic Societies (2002 to 2009), and international trial registries. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trials comparing propofol to placebo, no treatment, or other sedative, anaesthetic, or analgesic agents (used alone or in combination) in neonates undergoing procedures. Data collection and analysis were performed using the standard methods of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. One open-label randomised controlled trial involving 63 neonates met the inclusion criteria. In this trial, 33 neonates received propofol, while 30 neonates were treated with a combination of morphine, atropine, and suxamethonium. The results showed no statistically significant difference in the proportion of neonates requiring multiple intubation attempts between the two groups (39% in the propofol group versus 57% in the morphine-atropine-suxamethonium group; relative risk [RR] 1.40, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.85 to 2.29). However, the time required to prepare the medication, complete the procedure, and recover to the previous clinical status was shorter in the propofol group. No significant differences in clinically relevant side effects were observed between the groups, although the number of adverse events was small. The authors concluded that the current evidence is insufficient to make practice recommendations regarding the use of propofol in neonates. Further research is necessary to better understand the pharmacokinetics of propofol in this population. Once a relatively safe dose is established, additional randomised controlled trials are needed to assess the safety and efficacy of propofol in neonates.
